source.title_on_document: Neural Mechanisms of Collaborative Creative Thinking in Engineering Design: Human-Human Versus Human-AI Interaction

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplement or online appendix. Behavioral results appear only in Fig. 2 and two p-values in the text (PDF p. 5).

paper_design_summary: Fourteen male engineering students in Japan did an engineering divergent-thinking task under three within-subject conditions: alone, with another human, and with the help of GPT-4; the order was counterbalanced between subjects. Two creativity researchers rated each idea for originality and usefulness on 5-point scales, and EEG recorded brain activity during idea generation.

studies.label: Within-subject EEG experiment: individual vs human-human vs human-AI divergent thinking

assignment.what_was_assigned: Every participant did all three conditions (Individual, Human-Human, Human-AI); the order of conditions was counterbalanced between subjects. The paper does not say the order was random.
assignment.quote: All experimental participants performed the following three conditions. The order of implementation of the conditions was counterbalanced between subjects.

arms.name: Individual
arms.description: An engineering design task that required divergent thinking performed by a single individual on their own.

arms.name: Human-Human
arms.description: Two persons performed the engineering task together.

arms.name: Human-AI
arms.description: An individual performed the engineering task with the help of AI (GPT-4).

participants.exclusions: None reported. Results are described as for the 14 participants. Two participants took part in each experimental session (7 sessions implied, not stated).
participants.who: Male engineering students, healthy, all right-handed (Flanders Handedness Test).
participants.country: Japan (University of Tokyo ethics approval; participant country not stated explicitly)
participants.quote: Fourteen male students of engineering participated in this study. All students were healthy with no brain-related diseases or disabilities; two participants participated in each experiment.
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 330), Sect. 2.1 Participants; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3

ai_tool.how_used: The paper says only that the individual performed the task with the help of AI (GPT-4). Each cycle had an idea recognition phase (10 s) in which the participant read the idea of the partner or of the AI, so the AI appears to supply an idea per cycle. The interface and prompting are not described.

task.description: Engineering design task requiring divergent thinking: open-ended product solutions to societal problems (e.g., a product to reduce the space needed to store glass products at home before recycling). Phases: problem recognition (30 s), divergent thinking (30 s), idea output by typing (30 s), idea recognition (10 s); phases 2-4 repeated 10 times per problem.
task.duration: 30 s thinking + 30 s typing + 10 s reading per cycle, 10 cycles per problem; whole session including EEG setup within two hours. Number of problems per condition not stated.

outcomes.name: Usefulness of ideas (5-point expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two creativity researchers rated each idea on a 5-point scale for how useful the idea is to society as a whole (reasonable and useful). Inter-rater agreement not reported. Mean scores per condition shown in Fig. 2; compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

contrasts.reported: Wilcoxon signed-rank test: "the usefulness score was higher in the Human-AI condition than in the individual condition (p = 0.023)". Fig. 2 marks * (p < 0.05). Means shown only as bars with error bars; no numeric means, SDs, or test statistic printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2

contrasts.reported: No test reported for Human-AI vs Human-Human; Fig. 2 shows similar bars with no significance mark. (Human-Human vs Individual: p = 0.084, marked with a dagger, p < 0.1.)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas (5-point expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two creativity researchers rated each idea on a 5-point scale from 1 (not original at all) to 5 (very original): an intelligent response that others could not come up with. Mean scores per condition shown in Fig. 2; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

contrasts.reported: "The originality scores did not differ between conditions." No p-value or numeric means printed; Fig. 2 bars at similar heights in all three conditions with no significance mark.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2

contrasts.reported: "The originality scores did not differ between conditions." No statistics printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Sect. 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2

company_involvement.description: The study was part of a collaborative research project with Ricoh Company, Ltd.; coauthor Yukihisa Yokoyama (YY) is a Ricoh employee.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 335), Disclosure of Interests; PDF p. 1, affiliations

eligibility.reason: Within-subject lab experiment with only 14 participants, far below 50. The order of conditions was counterbalanced, but the paper does not say it was randomized. The outcomes (expert-rated originality and usefulness of ideas) are scored on output. List in the screening report as a small experiment.

one_line_finding: With 14 engineering students, ideas produced with GPT-4 were rated more useful than ideas produced alone (Wilcoxon p = 0.023), while originality did not differ across the individual, human-human, and human-AI conditions (PDF p. 5; Fig. 2 on PDF p. 6).
open_questions: Whether a counterbalanced condition order (not stated as randomized) satisfies criterion 1; moot here because N = 14.
How the human-AI interaction worked (prompting, whether GPT-4 supplied one idea per cycle) is not described.
notes: The paper's main outcomes are EEG source-localization contrasts (eLORETA, Fig. 3), which are not scored on output and are not listed. Behavioral results give no numeric means, SDs, test statistics, or number of ideas. The unit of the Wilcoxon test is not stated; participant-level means are assumed from the phrase 'mean scores ... for the ideas by the 14 participants'. In the Human-Human condition two participants work together, so that arm's output is joint.
